summary: Melatonin is the endogenous pineal hormone that regulates the sleep-wake (circadian) cycle. It is used to treat insomnia (notably short-term primary insomnia in older adults as a prolonged-release 2 mg product), jet lag, and sleep-onset problems, and in delayed sleep-wake phase and certain pediatric neurodevelopmental sleep disorders under specialist care. In the US it is sold OTC as a dietary supplement (no FDA drug label); in the EU prolonged-release melatonin is a licensed medicine. Typical doses are 1-5 mg taken 30-60 minutes before bedtime. It is generally well tolerated with mainly mild, transient effects.
indications: Short-term treatment of primary insomnia (e.g., prolonged-release 2 mg in adults >=55 years)
Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder and circadian-rhythm sleep disturbance
Sleep-onset insomnia in children/adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders (specialist use)

moa: Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland in darkness and signals the body's circadian clock to promote sleep. It binds MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, reducing the alerting signal and phase-shifting the sleep-wake cycle, thereby promoting sleep onset and resetting circadian rhythm.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to melatonin or product components
relative: Use with other sedatives or alcohol

preg: Avoid; safety in pregnancy has not been established due to insufficient data.
lact: Avoid; endogenous melatonin passes into breast milk and supplementation data are insufficient.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is established; use with caution.
hepatic: Clearance is reduced in hepatic impairment, leading to higher levels and prolonged effect; use with caution and avoid in significant impairment.

major: Fluvoxamine (strong CYP1A2 inhibitor) - markedly raises melatonin levels; avoid combination
moderate: CNS depressants / benzodiazepines / alcohol - additive sedation
CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, oral contraceptives) - increase melatonin levels
CYP1A2 inducers (carbamazepine, rifampin, smoking) - decrease melatonin levels and efficacy
interactions.food: Prolonged-release products are taken after food; food can affect absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; alcohol reduces the sleep-promoting effect and adds to sedation.

serious: Excessive sedation (especially with other CNS depressants)
emergency: Severe allergic reaction (facial swelling, difficulty breathing) - very rare

monitoring: Continued need for therapy (use short term where possible)
counsel: Take 30-60 minutes before bedtime and avoid bright light/screens afterward
Do not drive or operate machinery if you feel drowsy the next day
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives while using it
Use good sleep habits; it works best for sleep timing/jet lag and short-term insomnia
Swallow prolonged-release tablets whole and tell your doctor about other medicines
pk: Plasma peak ~0.5-1.5 h (IR); delayed with prolonged-release
A few hours; PR formulation extends overnight coverage
Store at room temperature, protected from light
pearls: Sold OTC as a dietary supplement in the US (no FDA drug label); prolonged-release melatonin is a licensed medicine in the EU - this record uses EMA/SmPC, BNF and standard references
Best for circadian problems (jet lag, delayed sleep phase) and short-term insomnia, especially in older adults
Timing matters more than dose - take 30-60 min before the desired sleep time
Avoid with fluvoxamine and minimize other sedatives/alcohol
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary time
missed: If a bedtime dose is missed and it is still well before the intended sleep time, it may be taken; otherwise skip it - do not take it in the middle of the night or take a double dose.
overdose: Overdose is usually mild - excessive drowsiness, headache and disorientation. There is no specific antidote; effects resolve with time. Provide supportive care and avoid activities requiring alertness until recovered.
